concept.name: Central limit order book
concept.definition: A market structure in which order flow in an instrument is centralized in a single transparent electronic limit order book at one venue, where a matching engine automatically matches orders to buy and sell under uniform priority rules, providing a single point of price discovery and queue priority.
concept.intuition: Instead of liquidity being scattered across many venues, every order joins one consolidated queue, so all participants see and compete in the same book.
concept.mechanics: Participants route orders through standardized messaging to the venue's matching engine, which applies the product's matching algorithm (e.g. FIFO or pro rata) and disseminates a market feed to all participants simultaneously. Futures markets such as CME Group's DCMs operate this way, in contrast to fragmented US equity trading across exchanges, ATSs, and internalizers.
concept.failure_modes: Centralization creates a single point of technological failure and a venue monopoly over fees and market data; even CLOB markets retain off-book liquidity in blocks and RFQ protocols. Consolidated depth can still vanish in stress events.
concept.misconceptions: A central limit order book does not guarantee deep or stable liquidity, and it does not eliminate hidden trading interest or latency advantages among participants.
concept.example: E-mini S&P 500 futures trade overwhelmingly on CME Globex's single central limit order book, whereas a US-listed stock trades across a dozen exchanges and dozens of off-exchange venues.

citations.source: CFTC, Concept Release on Risk Controls and System Safeguards for Automated Trading Environments, 78 FR 56542
citations.section: Part II.A.1 Automated Order Generation and Execution (DCM matching engines)
